items.text: Deployment model is deliberate and documented (SQL Server / Azure SQL MI / Azure SQL DB) with rationale
Environment separation exists (Dev / Test / Prod) with isolated instances or databases
Server/database topology documented (instances, databases, elastic pools)
Compute tier / service tier appropriate for workload (vCore/DTU, Business Critical/General Purpose)
Architecture diagram exists and reflects the actual implementation
Single source of truth — no duplicate warehouses serving the same purpose
Capacity/scale approach documented (scale-up vs scale-out, read replicas)
Clear layering defined (staging → ODS/integration → dimensional DW → data marts)
Each layer has a defined purpose and transformation responsibility
Staging area is transient/isolated and not queried by consumers
Data flow lineage is traceable end-to-end from source to mart
Schema separation used to organize layers/domains (dedicated schemas, not all in dbo)
Audit metadata captured on load (load_date, source_system, batch_id)
Historical/archival strategy defined for the DW
HA approach defined and matches SLA (Always On AG / failover cluster / zone-redundant / failover groups)
Redundancy configured for the production database (replicas / zone redundancy)
Read-scale replicas used for reporting where appropriate
Failover behavior documented and tested
Connection strings use listener / failover-group endpoints (not a single node)
Maintenance windows and patching approach defined (or Microsoft-managed for PaaS)

Application connection endpoint is a failover-aware **AG Listener** / FCI virtual network name — not a static client alias or DNS CNAME that must be manually repointed on failover (verify what the alias `C1SVPMLSQLAPP01` actually resolves to)
Multi-subnet AG connections use `MultiSubnetFailover=True` with an appropriate connect timeout in application connection strings
Alias / DNS resolution and failover behavior documented and validated — applications reconnect transparently on failover with no manual repoint
HA node configuration parity verified — both nodes have identical instance configuration, trace flags, MAXDOP/memory, logins, SQL Agent jobs, linked servers, and certificates
ETL tooling is consistent and deliberate (SSIS / Azure Data Factory / T-SQL / other)
ETL packages/pipelines follow consistent naming conventions
ETL is parameterized (no hardcoded servers, paths, dates, or credentials)
Orchestration/dependency management exists (master package/pipeline or scheduler)
Reusable/templated ETL components (no copy-paste per table)
ETL is metadata-driven or well-modularized where appropriate
ETL is logically documented (data flow, transformations, source-to-target mappings)
Incremental load implemented where applicable (watermark / CDC / Change Tracking)
Full load reserved for small reference/dimension tables or initial loads
Watermark/control values persisted reliably (control table, not volatile)
CDC / Change Tracking configured and maintained correctly where used
Insert/Update/Delete operations handled correctly (MERGE or equivalent)
Late-arriving / out-of-order data handled without corruption
ETL has structured error handling (TRY...CATCH, event handlers, failure paths)
Failed loads are restartable from point of failure (not full re-run)
Bad/rejected rows routed to a quarantine/error table (not silently dropped or failing the batch)
Retry logic exists for transient failures
ETL runs are idempotent (re-run does not duplicate data)
Failures trigger notifications (email/alert/monitoring)
Bulk load patterns used (BULK INSERT / bcp / minimal logging) for large loads
Set-based operations preferred over row-by-row processing
Indexes/constraints managed during large loads (disable/rebuild where beneficial)
ETL windows avoid contention with reporting/query workloads
ETL execution times monitored and baselined
Parallelism used appropriately (no unnecessary serial execution)
Consistent formatting and naming conventions across objects
No `SELECT *` in production code; explicit column lists
Schema-qualified object references (dbo.Table, not Table)
`SET NOCOUNT ON` and appropriate SET options in procedures
No deprecated syntax/features (e.g., old-style joins, `TEXT`/`NTEXT`)
Code is commented for complex logic; business rules explained
No hardcoded literals for environment-specific values
Business/transformation logic encapsulated in stored procedures/functions (not ad-hoc scripts)
Set-based logic used; cursors/`WHILE` loops avoided except where justified
Scalar UDFs avoided in hot paths (inlined/replaced where they hurt performance)
Views used appropriately (no deeply nested view chains that hide cost)
Dynamic SQL, where used, is parameterized (sp_executesql) — no injection risk
Temp tables vs table variables chosen appropriately for cardinality
Transactions scoped correctly (not held open across long operations)
`TRY...CATCH` with proper error raising/logging (THROW/RAISERROR)
`XACT_ABORT` / transaction state handling correct on error
Appropriate isolation levels used (no unnecessary SERIALIZABLE; RCSI considered)
Deadlock-prone patterns avoided; retry logic where needed
Multi-step operations maintain consistency on partial failure
Modeling approach is deliberate (3NF integration layer and/or dimensional marts)
Naming conventions consistent for tables, columns, and schemas
Data types appropriate and right-sized (no oversized varchar, correct numeric precision)
No stringly-typed dates/numbers; correct temporal types
Audit columns present where needed (created/modified, source, batch)
Schemas used to organize objects by layer/domain
Star schema implemented (fact + dimension tables, not flat wide tables)
Fact table grain clearly defined and documented per fact
Fact tables contain only foreign keys and measures (no descriptive attributes)
Surrogate keys used for dimensions (IDENTITY/sequence), not business keys in facts
Conformed dimensions shared across facts (no duplicate versions)
Date/Time dimension exists with required attributes
SCD strategy defined and implemented per dimension (Type 1/2/3)
SCD Type 2 valid_from/valid_to/is_current maintained correctly (where used)
Every table has an appropriate clustered index (or deliberate heap justification)
Columnstore indexes used for large fact tables / analytical workloads where appropriate
Nonclustered indexes align with query/workload patterns (not arbitrary)
No redundant/duplicate/overlapping indexes
Unused indexes identified and removed (DMV evidence)
Missing-index recommendations reviewed (not blindly applied)
Fill factor and index options set deliberately where needed
Index maintenance (rebuild/reorganize) scheduled based on fragmentation
Partitioning strategy defined for large tables (by date/range) where beneficial
Partition alignment supports fast load/switch and purge (sliding window)
Filegroups used to organize storage where applicable (SQL Server/MI)
Data compression (row/page/columnstore) applied where beneficial
tempdb configured appropriately (multiple files, sizing) — SQL Server/MI
Storage growth monitored; autogrowth settings sane (fixed size, not tiny %)
Archival/purge process exists for aged data
Primary keys defined on all tables
Foreign keys enforced where integrity matters (or documented trusted-by-ETL exceptions)
Unique constraints on natural/business keys where appropriate
Check constraints enforce domain rules where practical
Constraints are TRUSTED (not disabled/untrusted, which hurts the optimizer)
NOT NULL applied to mandatory columns
Data quality framework formally defined with rules, ownership, and scoring
DQ rules codified (config-driven or reusable procedures), not ad-hoc manual checks
DQ KPIs defined: completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency, uniqueness, validity
DQ results logged and trended over time
DQ remediation workflow exists (alert → investigate → fix → verify)
DQ SLAs defined per data product / mart
DQ failures halt progression where critical (bad data not silently promoted)
Quarantine pattern: failed rows routed to error tables with failure reason
Schema validation on inbound data (column presence, types)
Completeness: all expected sources/batches received
Record count reconciliation vs. source control counts
Duplicate detection across batches
Null/empty handling: unexpected nulls flagged
Corrupt/malformed rows isolated (not failing the entire batch)
Source metadata captured (load timestamp, source, batch ID)
Referential integrity validated (FKs in facts match dimensions)
Business rule validation applied (domain rules, ranges)
Deduplication verified — no duplicate business keys after load
Aggregate consistency: detail sums equal aggregate totals
Cross-layer reconciliation (mart vs integration vs source counts)
Unknown/default dimension member usage monitored
No duplicate grain in fact tables
Freshness validation: marts updated within SLA
**Dates**: valid ranges; consistent handling; no invalid future dates where prohibited
**Numeric / Financial**: precision preserved; no rounding errors; currency codes valid
**String / Text**: encoding/collation consistent; max length respected; no silent truncation
**Sensitive data**: masked/protected where required; format validation applied
**Categorical / Enum**: values within expected domain; no invalid codes
**Identifiers / Keys**: uniqueness verified; format consistent; no nulls in keys
**Boolean / Flag**: only expected values; consistent representation across tables
Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication used where possible (over SQL auth)
Principle of least privilege applied to logins/users (no broad db_owner/sysadmin)
Database roles used for permission grants (not per-user grants)
Application connects via a dedicated least-privilege service account/identity (Managed Identity preferred)
No shared/generic accounts for administrative or application access
Guest/contractor access explicitly governed and time-bound
Regular access reviews scheduled and documented
Schema/object-level permissions align with least privilege
Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) enabled for encryption at rest
TLS enforced for data in transit (Encrypt=true; minimum TLS version set)
Always Encrypted used for highly sensitive columns where required
Dynamic Data Masking applied to sensitive columns where appropriate
Row-Level Security implemented where multi-tenant/segmented access is required
Sensitive data classified (SQL Data Discovery & Classification / labels)
Backups are encrypted
Customer-managed keys (CMK/BYOK) used where policy requires
Firewall / network rules restrict access to known sources
Private endpoints / VNet integration used (Azure SQL) or network isolation (SQL Server)
Public network access disabled or tightly restricted (Azure SQL)
No broad "allow Azure services" / 0.0.0.0 firewall rules
Jump-host/bastion or controlled path for administrative access
Connection strings/secrets stored in a secret store (Key Vault), not config files or code
No credentials hardcoded in ETL packages, scripts, or linked servers
Managed Identity used for service-to-service auth where supported
Credential/key rotation policy defined and automated
Linked servers / external data sources use least-privilege, non-personal credentials
Applicable regulatory/compliance regime(s) identified and documented
In-scope regulated data categories identified and inventoried
Regime-specific control set mapped into the compliance matrix
Data residency / regional processing requirements identified and met
Required agreements in place (e.g., DPA) covering the platform and services
Breach / incident notification process documented
Segregation of Duties enforced (developer ≠ deployer ≠ approver)
All schema/code changes go through formal change management
Audit trail for changes to financial-relevant data
Access control changes logged and reviewable
Transformation logic documented and reproducible
Source-to-target reconciliation exists for financial data
Retention of historical financial data per policy
Personal data inventory exists with legal basis (if personal data is processed)
Data minimization applied — only necessary personal data stored
Right-to-erasure / rectification technically achievable
Data retention policies defined per data category
Consent / purpose tracking integrated where applicable
Cross-border transfer justified and documented (if applicable)
SQL Audit (server/database) enabled for sensitive operations
Login/permission changes captured and reviewable
Data access to sensitive tables auditable (who accessed what, when)
Audit logs retained per compliance requirement
Audit logs stored in a tamper-resistant location (separate store / immutable)
Temporal tables / change tracking used for data history where required
Source-to-target lineage documented (ETL mappings)
Enterprise catalog (e.g., Microsoft Purview) integrated or planned
Objects tagged/classified with business domain and owner
Dependencies documented (linked servers, cross-database references)
Extended properties / documentation on key objects
Every table/dataset has a defined data owner
Data stewards assigned per domain/subject area
Ownership documented — not tribal knowledge
Escalation path for data quality issues defined
DBA/ops ownership and responsibilities defined
Data dictionary exists for DW/mart tables
Technical metadata (schema) captured and current
Business definitions/rules documented and current
Metadata accessible to consumers (discoverable)
Business glossary / terminology maintained
Backup strategy defined and matches RPO (full/differential/log or PaaS automated)
Point-in-time restore capability verified (retention period appropriate)
Backups restore-tested regularly (not just taken)
Long-term retention (LTR) configured where required
Backups stored redundantly / geo-redundant where required
Backup failures alerted and monitored
Recovery model appropriate (Full/Simple/Bulk-logged) — SQL Server/MI
RTO and RPO defined and documented
HA solution matches SLA (Always On AG / failover groups / zone redundancy)
Geo-replication / failover group configured for DR where required
DR runbook documented
Failover tested at least annually
Secondary region/replica capacity provisioned or evaluated
Application connection resilience verified (retry logic, failover endpoints)
Availability mode (synchronous vs asynchronous commit) and failover mode (automatic vs manual) documented and aligned to RPO/RTO
AG / cluster health and replica synchronization state actively monitored — unhealthy or not-synchronizing replicas alerted
WSFC quorum / witness configured correctly for the node count (avoids split-brain); quorum model documented
Backup preference configured (backups taken from the preferred / secondary replica where used) and validated across failover
Listener / alias failover tested end-to-end — applications reconnect transparently with no manual intervention
Consistency checks (DBCC CHECKDB) scheduled and monitored (SQL Server/MI)
Page verification set to CHECKSUM
Corruption detection alerting in place
ETL is idempotent — safe to re-run after failure
Multi-step operations maintain integrity on partial failure
Data freshness SLAs defined per mart/data product
Load completion SLAs set and monitored
SLA breach triggers alerts
Historical SLA compliance tracked and reported
Monitoring solution in place (Azure Monitor / SQL Insights / third-party)
Key metrics tracked (CPU, memory, IO, DTU/vCore, waits)
Resource utilization trended over time
Alerts configured for resource saturation and errors
Long-running/blocking query alerting configured
Dashboard accessible to operations (not just DBAs)
Query Store enabled and configured appropriately
Query Store used to detect regressions and force plans where needed
DMVs used for ongoing performance analysis (waits, missing/unused indexes)
Wait statistics reviewed as part of routine tuning
Baselines captured for comparison over time
Extended Events sessions used for diagnostics (over deprecated Profiler traces)
Deadlock capture configured
Error/severity alerts configured (Agent alerts or equivalent)
Alert thresholds tuned to avoid fatigue
Escalation path defined for critical alerts
ETL/job run history captured and retained
Job failures alert the responsible team
Job duration trends monitored
SQL Agent / scheduler jobs inventoried and owned
Log/rowcount reconciliation captured per ETL run
Database schema and code source-controlled (SSDT/SQL project or migration scripts)
ETL packages/pipelines source-controlled
Branching strategy defined (feature/main/release)
Pull request reviews required before merge
Commit messages descriptive and linked to work items
Secret-scanning enabled on the repository
Automated build of the database project (DACPAC or migrations)
Automated deployment pipeline (Dev → Test → Prod)
Schema drift detected and reconciled between environments
No manual production changes — all via pipeline
Deployment approvals required (segregation of duties)
Rollback / recovery procedure defined and tested
Pre/post-deployment scripts managed and idempotent
Separate Dev / Test / Prod environments
Production access restricted (no developer write/deploy)
Test environment representative of production (data, scale)
Environment configuration parity maintained
Non-prod data masking/subsetting applied where sensitive
Unit tests exist for critical transformation logic (e.g., tSQLt)
Integration tests validate end-to-end ETL
Data validation tests run post-deployment (counts, schema checks)
Performance tests exist for critical queries/loads
Regression testing on schema changes
Service tier / compute sizing based on workload analysis (not guesswork)
DTU/vCore utilization profiled (peak vs off-peak)
Elastic pools used where multiple databases share capacity efficiently
Auto-scaling / serverless considered where workload is intermittent
Growth projections modeled for next 6–12 months
Storage sizing and growth monitored
Reserved capacity / savings plans evaluated vs pay-as-you-go
Right-sizing reviewed periodically (over-provisioned tiers reduced)
Non-prod environments scaled down / paused when idle
Backup storage costs monitored (retention tuned)
Unused databases/objects/indexes cleaned up
Compression used to reduce storage and IO cost where beneficial
Architecture overview document exists
Data flow / source-to-target mappings documented
Business rules for transformations documented outside code
Known issues and tech debt registered
Runbook exists for daily/weekly/monthly operations
Failure recovery procedures documented step-by-step
On-call / escalation procedures documented
Maintenance procedures documented (index/stats/integrity)
Table/column definitions documented with business context
Source-to-target mapping documented per table
Acronyms and business terminology glossary available
Documentation kept current with schema changes
Solution maintainable by someone other than the original builder
No single point of human dependency (bus factor > 1)
Onboarding materials exist for new team members
Code is self-documenting or well-commented for complex logic
Critical queries reviewed via execution plans (no unexpected scans/spools)
SARGable predicates used (no functions wrapping indexed columns)
Set-based rewrites applied where cursors/loops caused poor plans
Implicit conversions eliminated (data-type mismatches in joins/filters)
Excessive/unnecessary sorts and spools addressed
Key lookups minimized via covering indexes where beneficial
Query hints used sparingly and documented where present
Index usage analyzed (seeks vs scans) against workload
Missing indexes reviewed and applied judiciously
Unused/duplicate indexes removed
Fragmentation-based maintenance (rebuild/reorganize) automated
Columnstore health maintained (rowgroup quality, tuple mover) where used
Fill factor tuned for volatile tables where needed
Blocking monitored and root causes addressed
Deadlocks captured (Extended Events) and resolved
Appropriate isolation level / RCSI or snapshot isolation considered
Long transactions avoided; batch large operations
Lock escalation understood and mitigated where problematic
Reporting workloads isolated from write workloads (read replicas) where possible
tempdb sized and file-configured correctly (SQL Server/MI)
tempdb contention monitored and mitigated
Resource Governor used where workload isolation is required (where supported)
MAXDOP and cost threshold for parallelism set deliberately
Memory grants monitored (no excessive spills to tempdb)
Statistics kept current (auto-update on, plus manual updates after large loads)
Auto-create statistics enabled where appropriate
Parameter sniffing issues identified and mitigated (OPTIMIZE FOR, recompile, etc.)
Plan cache health reviewed (no excessive single-use plans / bloat)
Query Store used to force stable plans where regressions occur
